note: Self-Delimiting Numeric Values, RFC 5050 clause 4.1, adopted by CCSDS 734.1-B-1 via RFC 5326 clause 1.6 item 20. Seven value bits per octet, most significant group first; every octet but the last carries the continuation bit 0x80. The seven cases below are the worked examples RFC 5050 prints; the wide cases after them are derived from the same rule and Values are decimal strings where they exceed 2^53, per the corpus convention.

encode.name: zero
encode.note: A single octet with no continuation bit and seven zero value bits.

encode.name: one
encode.note: RFC 5050 clause 4.1 worked example: 1 fits one octet.

encode.name: largest-single-octet
encode.note: RFC 5050 clause 4.1 worked example: 0x7f is the largest value with seven bits, so still one octet and no continuation bit.

encode.name: first-two-octet-value
encode.note: RFC 5050 clause 4.1 worked example: 0x80 needs eight bits, so two octets. High group is 1 with the continuation bit set (0x81), low group is 0 (0x00).

encode.name: two-octet-value-81
encode.note: RFC 5050 clause 4.1 worked example: 0x81 = high group 1 (0x81 with continuation), low group 1 (0x01).

encode.name: three-octet-value-4234
encode.note: RFC 5050 clause 4.1 worked example: 0x4234 splits into seven-bit groups 1, 4, 0x34 -> 0x81 0x84 0x34, the first two carrying the continuation bit.

encode.name: three-octet-value-7fff
encode.note: RFC 5050 clause 4.1 worked example: 0x7fff splits into groups 1, 0x7f, 0x7f -> 0x81 0xff 0x7f.

encode.name: largest-two-octet-value
encode.note: 0x3fff is the largest value two octets can carry (fourteen value bits): groups 0x7f, 0x7f -> 0xff 0x7f. Derived from the seven-bits-per-octet rule and the continuation bit: each octet gives up its high bit, so two octets leave fourteen for the value and 0x4000 needs a third.

encode.name: first-three-octet-value
encode.note: 0x4000 is one past what two octets hold, so three octets: groups 1, 0, 0 -> 0x81 0x80 0x00.

encode.name: max-uint32
encode.note: 2^32-1 needs 32 value bits, so five octets: groups 0x0f, 0x7f, 0x7f, 0x7f, 0x7f -> 0x8f 0xff 0xff 0xff 0x7f.

encode.name: max-uint64
encode.note: 2^64-1 needs 64 value bits. At seven bits per octet that is ten octets, the maximum an SDNV carrying a 64-bit value can reach: groups 1 then nine groups of 0x7f -> 0x81 followed by eight 0xff and a final 0x7f. Written as a decimal string because a JSON number cannot hold it.

decode.name: zero-inverse
decode.note: One octet with no continuation bit decodes to its seven value bits and consumes exactly one octet.

decode.name: three-octet-value-4234-inverse
decode.note: The inverse of the 0x4234 worked example: three octets, the first two carrying continuation bits.

decode.name: max-uint64-inverse
decode.note: The inverse of max-uint64: ten octets decode to 2^64-1 and consume all ten.

decode.name: stops-at-the-first-octet-without-continuation
decode.note: SDNVs are self-delimiting, so a decoder reads one value and reports how much it used, leaving the rest for the next field. Here 0x01 decodes to 1 having consumed one octet, with 0xff 0xff untouched.

reject.name: ends-mid-value
reject.note: Every octet sets the continuation bit, so the value never terminates before the data does. A decoder must not get past octet 2: every octet sets the continuation bit and the input ends.

reject.name: longer-than-ten-octets
reject.note: Eleven continuation octets run past the ten-octet maximum a 64-bit SDNV can occupy, so a decoder must refuse rather than wrap.
